claims.text: A thin WS2 coating deposited on a high-entropy-alloy surface will provide self-lubricating behavior.
The WS2 coating will reduce the coefficient of friction relative to the untreated alloy.
The WS2 coating will reduce wear rate relative to the untreated alloy.
PVD can produce a uniform, adherent WS2 film on the high-entropy alloy.
The coating should remain effective from near room temperature to several hundred degrees Celsius under typical moving-component contact loads.
WS2 has a layered crystalline structure that facilitates interlayer sliding.
The WS2 coating acts as a barrier to direct contact between surface asperities.
Easy shear between WS2 layers reduces friction.
The WS2 film protects the alloy substrate by absorbing and distributing contact stresses.
The chemical stability of WS2 helps maintain low friction at elevated temperatures.
The coated samples will exhibit approximately a 20–30% reduction in coefficient of friction under identical operating conditions across the tested temperature range.
The coated samples will exhibit nearly a 50% reduction in wear rate under identical operating conditions across the tested temperature range.
Coating effectiveness may diminish above the thermal-stability limit of WS2 because of oxidation or degradation.
Coating effectiveness may diminish under extreme contact pressures.
Coating adhesion and uniformity are critical to achieving the predicted tribological improvements.
Existing data on WS2 coatings applied to high-entropy alloys under varying thermal conditions are limited.
Failure to meet the specified friction and wear reductions across the evaluated temperature range, or coating degradation or delamination under those conditions, will falsify the hypothesis.
